findings.where: Screen 5 (The cube) text, screen 6 (Half speed), explain paragraph 2 and the ignores line
findings.what: The half-speed load of 0.125 is given as a fact, yet the lesson's own source says the propeller law 'works well' in steady high-speed running but 'breaks down' at partial loading, 'such as at a slower speed' (SSRN, notes 7.4); the brief also promised to teach it as a model, and the ignores line gives a different reason with no source (hull, sea, loading). Fix: add the cited caveat, or base the 12.5% puzzle on the fan affinity law, whose quote says exactly 'slowing a fan to 50% speed reduces the power used to 12.5%' (ScienceDirect, notes 7.4, also in the brief), and keep the propeller law as the marine case with its caveat.

'a gas's pressure against its volume has this shape too' leaves out the explain's 'a fixed amount of gas at a fixed temperature', and without it the claim is false for the compressions he will meet in applied heat (pV^n = C, notes 3.3). Add 'at a fixed temperature'.

'On the square it cuts twice' is contradicted on the same screen: the level line can be dragged to 0 (the table reads 'cuts once') and to −1 ('no cut'). Say 'anywhere above the bottom of the U', as the explain does, and name the result many-to-one (HELM, brief), because the screen names only one-to-one.

findings.where: Finish sentence and the explain's bold summary
findings.what: 'Five shapes come from what each rule does to a doubled input' claims too much. Doubling explains how fast each curve bends, but the U's mirror, the S's lower half, the one-over's two pieces and the root's starting edge come from what the rule does to negative inputs and to 0, which the screens do teach; say both.

findings.where: Screen 1 (The line) and screen 5 (The cube) text
findings.what: The finish and the practice rule of thumb rest on doubling, but the screens never say what doubling does on the line ('doubles it, through 0') or on the cube ('1 gives 1, 2 gives 8, so eight times'), and no gallery picture draws a doubled input; one clause each would close the thread that the square, one-over and root screens already carry.

'near 0 the point runs off up the side' holds only from the right, because from the left it runs off down. The screen also fits five ideas into one paragraph (halving, running off, no point at 0, the second curve, then 12 V and the gas); the gas can wait for screen 13.

'a flow meter at 50% of its pressure difference shows 71% of its flow' should say 'of its full pressure difference' and 'of its full flow', so the percentages read as shares of full scale, as screen 10 and the graph's axis titles do.
'nothing to its left' is stated without a reason or a pointer to one; add '(lesson 4 says why)', as the explain does, so the deferral is visible on screen.

findings.where: Screen 1 gallery law label under y = x
findings.what: 'Law: a transmitter's straight-line scale' sits under y = x, but the transmitter is S(p) = 0.16p + 4, which does not pass through 0. Label it as a line law, such as 'a transmitter's scale, y = mx + b', so it is not read as y = x.

findings.where: Screen 2 (Spot the line) and screen 13 (A gas squeezed)
findings.what: The gallery's tab row is drawn on both screens but does nothing. On screen 2 'line' is filled in, and on screen 13 the five names sit as plain text above the graph, where they read like a second set of answers; hide the row on both. At 360 px screen 2 also leaves about 130 px of empty scene between the tables and the answer buttons.

An electrician may reasonably pick '3 A only', because 3 A in either direction is still 3 A. Options written as inputs on the graph ('−3 A and 3 A', '3 A only', '4.5 A') would test reading down from both cuts of the level line, without the question turning on wording.
